seoDescription: Discover why monorepos are now an indispensable tool for modern TypeScript development. This video explores a developer's journey from frustration to advocacy, highlighting how tools like Bun and Vercel's Turborepo have revolutionized project architecture. Learn how to manage complex applications with multiple parts, such as a SvelteKit web app, a Raycast extension, and Cloudflare Workers, all within a single repository. See practical examples demonstrating how to share logic and streamline your build process for more ambitious and maintainable projects.

chapters.description: This chapter covers how Bun serves as an all-in-one package manager and runtime, simplifying monorepo dependency management with its native workspace support.

chapters.title: Core Tool 2: Turborepo for Task Running
chapters.description: This section introduces Vercel's Turborepo, highlighting its remote caching and the powerful `turbo dev` command for managing multiple development servers with a clean UI.

chapters.title: Example 2: The 'Better Context' Project
chapters.description: A look at the 'better-context' monorepo, which contains a CLI published to npm, a web app, and more, demonstrating advanced Turborepo usage with nested commands.

chapters.description: This chapter showcases the 'R8Y' project, focusing on how a shared database package encapsulates Drizzle logic for both a web app and a background worker.

chapters.description: A deep dive into Turborepo's `--filter` command, showing how it intelligently runs tasks on specific packages and their dependencies, which dramatically speeds up workflows.

chapters.description: The video concludes by reiterating that modern tooling has made monorepos powerful and accessible, encouraging developers to try them for their next ambitious project.

summary:
## From Monorepo Skeptic to Advocate

Monorepos were historically difficult to set up, but modern tooling has transformed them into a powerful and practical approach for building ambitious, multi-part applications. The developer now uses them for all significant projects.

## The Modern Monorepo Toolkit

Two primary tools have made monorepos significantly easier to work with:

- **Bun**: An all-in-one JavaScript toolkit used as the package manager, runtime, and script runner. Its robust, built-in support for **workspaces** is a cornerstone of this setup, replacing tools like `npm` or `pnpm`.

- **Turborepo**: A high-performance build system for monorepos from Vercel. Key features include:
    - **Task Running**: The `turbo dev` command, especially with the `--ui` flag, provides an interactive terminal UI to manage multiple concurrent services (e.g., a web frontend, a background worker, and a database service).
    - **Caching**: Intelligent caching of build outputs and tasks significantly speeds up local and CI/CD builds.
    - **Filtering**: Allows you to run commands on specific packages and their dependencies.

## Core Concepts & Patterns

- **Workspace Configuration**: In your root `package.json`, define the `workspaces` key to point to your applications and shared packages (e.g., `"workspaces": ["apps/*", "packages/*"]`).
- **Creating Shared Packages**: Isolate reusable logic (e.g., database schemas, API types, UI components) into a dedicated package within the `packages/` directory.
- **Local Package Linking**: Give your shared package a scoped name in its `package.json` (e.g., `"name": "@my-project/db"`). Then, in your application's `package.json`, add it as a dependency using the workspace protocol (e.g., `"@my-project/db": "workspace:*"`).
- **Importing Shared Code**: After running `bun install`, you can import from the shared package using its name, eliminating fragile relative paths: `import { schema } from '@my-project/db';`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Shared packages must properly export their modules from an entry point (e.g., `index.ts`) for other packages in the workspace to consume them correctly.

## Practical Project Examples

- **p-thing**: A project with a **SvelteKit** web app, a **Raycast extension**, and a **Cloudflare Worker**. All three components share logic from a central `@p-thing/convex` package.
- **better-context**: A complex system including a **CLI published to npm**, a web app, a server, and a Raycast extension, all managed within one repository.
- **r8y**: A YouTube management tool with a **SvelteKit web app** and a separate **background worker**. Both share a `@r8y/db` package that encapsulates all **Drizzle ORM** logic and database schemas.

## Advanced Techniques & Workflows

- **Nested Turbo Commands**: A `dev` script in one package can itself be a `turbo` command to orchestrate multiple sub-services, like running a Vite server and a Convex dev server simultaneously.
- **Efficient Filtering**: Use `turbo run <script> --filter=<package_name>` to execute tasks only on a specific package and its dependencies. Turborepo automatically includes dependencies in the task graph, ensuring correctness.

> [!TIP]
> Filtering is especially useful when working with AI coding agents. You can instruct an agent to run validation scripts (`check`, `format`) only on the packages it modified, saving significant time.

- **Optimized Deployments**: For containerized deployments, use `turbo prune --scope=<package_name>` to create a minimal copy of the monorepo containing only the files and dependencies needed for a specific application. This is ideal for smaller, faster Docker builds.
transcription:
## From Monorepo Skeptic to Advocate

For the longest time, I despised monorepos. They were a massive pain in the ass to actually try and work with. I just could not get over the hump of getting them set up. It was way too hard to get dependencies to work. Way too hard to get everything set up. Way too hard to figure out how to import something from a local package in your workspaces. None of it made sense. I didn't like it. So, I just gave up on it. I refused to use them for many, many years. All of my projects were just in a single codebase until recently. I finally gave them another shot. And now basically everything I build is a monorepo. Better context gigantic monorepo. R8yv3 giant monorepo. Pick thing 2.0 giant monorepo. Even the little demo that I did for my solidjs video that had a react example, a solid example and a spelt example. This was a monorepo. They are so unbelievably useful. And now that both bun and turborepo have become much more mature, they are totally feasible to use for all of your TypeScript projects. And at this point, I can't really imagine building without them. They just make so many things so much easier and they've really fed into me making my projects a lot more ambitious.

## Example 1: The 'p thing' Project

I want to use P thing as the first example here because it feels like the kind of thing that you wouldn't need a monor repo for. Like this is just a website that hosts a bunch of images, does some background removal stuff, adds in a nice little tagging system, and lets you manage some organizations and API keys. Like why the hell would you need to put this in a monor repo? But P thing also has a raycast extension. If I open up Raycast, I type in P thing and open it up, I now have access to all of my P thing assets stored within Raycast.

There's one package JSON for the web project, which is the Spellkit app. Then there's one for the Raycast app, which is what I just showed you. And I have another one here for the image optimizer worker, which is the Cloudflare worker that is powering the background removal. So when I toggle it to remove the background, that's not actually happening within the Spellkit app, that's just changing the URL, which is getting sent over to Cloudflare to return these images down at the proper sizing and with or without the background depending on which setting I have set here. That's another separate codebase. I'm hosting the Cellkit app on Railway and I'm hosting the Cloudflare worker on obviously Cloudflare because it's Cloudflare worker. I can now have all of that stuff shared within one project even though these are basically three different projects, but they're all part of P thing 2.0. So instead of having to have three different git repos that I have to constantly jump between and constantly manage and it just makes my environment hellish, now they're just in one place.

And when I do my bun rundev, I get this nice little UI with turbo repo that has the image optimizer, the raycast dev instance, the web instance, and I also have a package for convex. Convex in this project is being shared between raycast and web. I can make a convex package that has all of the convex stuff wrapped up nicely inside of it that I can then import into my web app, import into my raycast app, and it all just kind of works. It makes it so much easier to build complex apps and are actually really good at setting up and working with monor repos.

## Technical Deep Dive and Sponsor Segment

Now, I want to talk you guys through all the tech I'm using to do this. It's actually pretty simple. Some of the other ways that I'm abusing this in projects that aren't just like making more things in one thing and how the kind of dev experience for this actually flows. But before we do that, we need to hear from today's sponsor. 

I want to talk about Open Code, not because they're today's sponsor, but because it's one of the most useful pieces of technology out there right now. The only problem is running it in the cloud in the background is a massive pain in the ass, unless you're using something like today's sponsor, Daytona. Daytona has this really, really nice guide for build a coding agent using Open Code Web and Daytona. And once you or your LLM has got this set up, the end result is insanely simple. As you can see, all I need to do to put Open Code in the cloud is make an instance of Daytona, create the sandbox, install Open Code onto the sandbox, create the preview link, set up the preview URL pattern, set up the Open Code instance, and then we just grab the link. I'm going to go in here, do bun index.ts. It'll create the sandbox, install OpenCode. Give it a second here. Start the Open Code web server. It's not secured, but that's fine. Then we grab this guy, open the web interface, paste that in there, give it a second to spin up, and now we have a full Open Code instance running in the cloud. I'm just going to go to this root project. Uh, let's switch the model down to Sure, we'll do GLM 4.7. Make a new TS project. Use bun for the package manager. Now we have a cloud running sandbox with open code on it. You could build a background agent with this. You could do something like better context with this. You do literally anything you want, even just a normal agent that doesn't have anything to do with coding. That's just like doing some menial tasks in the background. Open code and cloud code are really good harnesses for that. Daytona makes it insanely easy to work with any of these. It's they've got guides for Langchain, Master, Claude Code, Codeex, the Google ADK, even the crazy new RLM stuff. They are on the bleeding edge of this stuff and you should very much be trying this stuff out at dav7.link/tona.

## Core Tool 1: Bun for Workspaces

The first piece you need for this is bun. I have completely replaced npm, pnpm, yarn, all of those different things with bun. It is my package manager. It is my runtime. It is my script runner. I am doing everything with bun at this point. And they finally fixed their monor repo support. For a very long time, if you wanted to do a monor repo sainely, you pretty much had to do it with pnpm workspaces. Now, bun just kind of handles workspaces right out of the box super super well. You can see I have this workspaces declaration within my root package JSON telling it like hey look inside of apps look inside of packages and these are the two workspaces within my project and then when I want to import a package into another package so like within apps web I have this dependency right here that is at pick/convex its version is just star because I'm not loading that off of npm itself I am loading that from this package in the same project based on its name. So I have named this pick thing/convex. I am exporting all of this stuff which is the key thing you need to do. You need to figure out what pieces you want to export from all of your packages. I'm exporting the API declaration, the data model declaration, the server types. And now that I have all of these, all I have to do to actually use this within the web app is import API from atpic thing/convex. So instead of doing it the normal way, which would be import API from dot dot dot dotconvexgenerated whatever, we're now just importing this API directly from that package. 

So if I change some type within that package, I instantly get that new type propagated out into the web app and into the actual raycast extension. You can also get nice helper types in here. You can basically just stick whatever the hell you want to inside of this thing. And it makes shared reusable logic across more complicated applications infinitely easier to do. And the last thing you need to do to get all this working with bun is literally just go into the root directory of your project where this package json is. Run bun install and then it's done. It will install all the local packages, link everything up correctly, and it will just kind of work right out of the box. It's really, really sick.

## Core Tool 2: Turborepo for Task Running

The other core piece of this is Turbo Repo. It is a project by Verscell that I think is actually one of the better projects they've shipped over the last few years. It's pretty much just a set of tools for your monor repo to make working with them easier. For one, they have a really nice caching solution, which I've actually started to lean on a bit more. It makes doing production builds easier. If I'm caching all my build steps in the cloud, so if I run build locally and then I run build in my deploy script again within my railway instance, it'll hit the remote cache, pull everything down instantly, and I get that like full turbo instant build. But the real reason I'm using it is for this `turbo dev` command right here. So the way I actually spun this project up is I just did bunddev and then this is going to do turbo dev which is going to spin up every single project within the workspaces that has a dev command. So all these different ones have their own dev command. I define the commands I want turbo to look for in here. So like this dev command I'm not caching anything remotely because it's a dev server. It is persistent and all that means is just that since I have my convex server, my web server, all that stuff is just going to persist the 2e up on screen for a while. And since I passed in this d- UI2 flag, I get this really great UI for viewing all the logs for all the stuff I'm working with.

Another weird thing I used this for that was really nice is I was setting up this example for the solid video I did a little bit ago that had a demo in spelt, a demo in solid, and a demo in React. All these demos did the exact same thing. It was just meant to showcase the differences between the frameworks. I put those in a monor repo here. I'm using turbo to run the dev command. So within my root package JSON, I'm doing `turbo dev --ui2`. So within my dev server, you can see I've spun up React, spun up spelt, spun up solid, and now instead of having to create three different repos to show off this example, and they're all wrapped up nicely into one single git repo that I can just send out and show you guys as an example.

## Example 2: The 'Better Context' Project

Another place where this is really useful is in another project I'm working on called better context, where I have this gigantic monor repo that has a CLI app that's being published to npm. I have a raycast extension which we just made earlier on stream. That was really fun. Speaking of which, I've started live recording these videos on stream. You should come check that out. Probably doing that like every Tuesday, Thursdayish of every week is kind of the target. We'll see how it works. I'll have the Twitch link down below. You should come hang out. It's a lot of fun. But then also we have the sandbox in here where I was playing around and testing some stuff. The server which is the actual server side implementation of BTCA. And then the web app which is the actual spelt project. And all of these work very differently. For example, the CLI itself gets published to npm. So I have the name on here as just BTCA. And this is the thing that's going up to npm. You can see in here I have this bin object within the package JSON. And that's saying that whenever you install this, you should run the bin.js file. That bin.js file is going to do a bunch of logic in here that's going to grab one of the pre-built bun binaries that I do at the build step that get shipped down with BTCA. When you do bun add `btca`, it'll install the native binaries for you. then the bingjs will pick the right one for your platform, get it going for you, and it'll just kind of work. But that's wrapped up in the same exact codebase as this spelt js website that is completely different and does completely different things. I don't have a root `bun dev` command for this one cuz everything works kind of differently, but they're super flexible.

It's basically just a way to stick all the things you need for a project in one place. So like for example, I have this script for dev web which will do `turbo dev --filter btca-web`. And what's really cool about this one is if you look at the package json in here, the dev script is actually another turbo script because I have turbo repo set up within this project within a turbo repo that will spin up both the convex dev server and the vit dev server for spelt in the same exact process. So if I do `bun dev web`, you'll see it's spinning up the web instance and it's spinning up the convex instance. So now both the convex dev server and the speltkit server are running at the exact same time together which makes developing this infinitely easier. That's another little thing too is like yes this is in a giant monor repo but even if I was just doing a single repo that is just a spelt app typically speaking I'm going to be working with something like convex where I need to have a separate dev server running for that you don't have to make multiple package jsons in order to get some value out of something like turbo repo. It basically just allows you to run a bunch of commands at once with a really nice UI wrapping all of it and some caching and stuff like that.

## Example 3: 'R8Y' and Shared DB Logic

Another one I'm using Monoros for is this project I've been working on called R8Y, which is like an internal channel management system for me and Theo that makes our lives a lot easier. One of the things I'm doing with this is I have this shared package here called DB. So I have R8Y/DB and all that's happening within this project is it's just encapsulating all of the logic for the DB. So you can see I have this dev script in here that is running Drizzle kit studio. I have a check command, a format command, which we're going to talk about those in a second. But the really important piece is I have this export up here of dot from/source/index.ts. Within this index.ts file, I am exporting everything from connection, exporting everything from types, exporting all the stuff from the install drizzle OM instance here. So I can import that in my other packages and use it correctly. And I'm exporting my schema. So like all the core drizzle management stuff which would typically live within some like lib/db folder within your nex.js app or spelt app now lives within its own self-contained little place that I can just work with directly that I can then reuse across a bunch of different apps because there are two apps in this project. One is for web. This is just the normal speltkit web app that you're seeing here. Nothing too crazy. But the bg one is very interesting because this is a background worker that I have set up to constantly run in a loop. It's basically just a cron job that every 20 minutes will sync my channel and Theo's channel with the YouTube API. Pull in new comments, parse those comments, check view counts, check for new publishes, send out notifications to me if I need them. And I can deploy both of these projects separately from the same monor repo to Railway. So you can see up here I have the background worker, which is the BG app, and then I have R8 web, which is the web app, both deployed up on their own really nicely. I even set this guy up so that I'm using Docker to build and deploy the actual images mostly just for fun because I wanted to test it. But it also shows one of the nice things that you can do with turbo repo which is it has this turborepo prune command which will basically just install only the packages you need for r8y/web. So I'm telling it, hey only grab me the stuff that I need for this specific package. It's going to grab all the packages it needs there. It's going to install the frozen lock file. It's going to do all the build step in here. And then it's finally going to publish this as a node instance that I can then serve through railway. And if you're wondering where the database for this guy lives, it's currently just sitting on a plan scale Postgress instance. They recently brought back the $5 a month Postgress instances which are really really sick. I wanted to test that out for this. I've been super happy with it. And I can just manage all of that stuff through my DB package and it just kind of works in these two. It's really really nice.

## Advanced Turborepo: Filtering and Caching

The filter keyword is one of the nicest parts about this whole setup too where you can see in my root package JSON for better context. I have a shitload of scripts like I have build all build CLI build web check all check CLI check web etc etc and I'm inside of these commands I am filtering down to just check the CLI here. So if I do bun check CLI that's only going to run the turbo on the actual CLI itself. But you can also see it's running the check on shared because Turbo is smart enough to see that BTCA shared and BTCA server are both dependencies of the CLI. When I run this check command on the actual CLI itself, it's going to first run it on shared and server. Then it'll run the check on the main instance itself and then actually do the thing. And since I'd already run this check command earlier today and I haven't changed anything, it just runs instantly. It's fully cached. Makes everything super fast and easy to work with. eliminates a lot of the pain that you would normally deal with in a monor repo of having everything just naturally be slower. 

There's a lot of ways to work around this stuff. And when you're using agents to build in code bases like this, the thing I've been doing is I update my agents MD to tell the agent that like, hey, here are all the packages that you have access to. And whenever you make changes in one of these packages, run its check script and its format script. So if it makes a change in CLI, it's going to run bun check CLI and then it's going to run bun format CLI. And the button check CLI command is just this `tsgo --no-emit` command because I'm using TSGO the new go rewrite of TypeScript which is coming hopefully very soon. It's going to make sure that nothing is currently wrong with it that it will compile. If something goes wrong, it'll throw a bunch of errors that the agent can then go fix. This is just a nice way to not have your agent check your entire project over and over again. You can filter it down to very specific pieces of your project.

## Conclusion: Monorepo Tooling is Ready

And as far as the repos I just showed off go, uh, R8Y is open source. Better context is open source. The spelt solid react compared is fully open source. P thing will eventually be open source, but really just if you want to take a look at kind of how I'm doing all this stuff and setting up my projects, they'll be linked down below and you can just kind of see how this works. 

Really, the point I wanted to get across in this kind of short video is just that modern repos are actually usable and good now. The tooling has finally caught up and they feel first class in a way that they just never really did before. and having them in all of my projects just makes it way easier for me to spin up new random things like a raycast extension or a one-off Cloudflare worker that will do some very useful thing that in the past would have been a hellish thing that I just wouldn't want to deal with so I'd find a way to engineer around it and just not work with it. Now I have no problems doing it. I think monoros are really dope. You should go try them. If you enjoyed this video, make sure you like and subscribe.
